modules.name: Array
modules.header:
A run of elements whose length is fixed when it is made and whose storage is on the heap.
`Array<T>` is what to reach for when the length is decided at run time and never changes afterwards. It is not
`T[N]`, whose length is part of its type and whose storage is wherever the value containing it lives; it is not
`T[..]`, which borrows storage someone else owns; and it is not `Vector<T>`, which can grow. Owning storage of
a length chosen at run time is the one thing none of the others does.
An array owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. Handing one to a function
requires an explicit move; reading the source afterwards is rejected while
compiling rather than discovered later. Destruction destroys every element and then releases the block, in that
order, so an array of things that own something does not leak what they own.
The allocator is injected at construction and kept. An array made from one allocator is released to the same one,
which is what lets an arena's arrays disappear with the arena and a pool's come back to the pool.
Every constructor copies its elements into the storage. A move-only element type cannot be copied, so an array of
those has to be built another way — `Vector<T>` and its `Push` is the shape that works, since each element is
moved in exactly once.

modules.name: BitSet
modules.header:
A set of small non-negative integers, one bit each.
The bits live in 64-bit words, so membership is a shift and a mask, counting is a population count per word, and
the set operations work a word at a time. The set grows when a bit past its length is set; reading a bit past the
length answers false rather than failing, since an absent bit is an unset one. Running out of memory while growing
terminates the program, as everywhere in this package.

modules.name: Capacity
modules.header:
Overflow-checked sizing arithmetic, shared by every container in this package so the checks exist once rather than
once per type.
Integer overflow wraps silently, so `count * sizeof(T)` is the single most dangerous expression a container
writes: a product that wraps asks the allocator for a small block and then writes far past it. Every allocation in
this package sizes itself through `ByteSize` rather than multiplying inline.
The checks are written out rather than reached for from `Core`, because each of these does something beyond the
arithmetic — choosing a growth, falling back when a doubling does not fit — and a checked multiply is one line
of that. What matters is that the dangerous product is never evaluated: `ByteSize` divides instead.
A size that cannot be represented is one no allocator could serve, so these throw `AllocError::Unsupported`, the
same error the allocator gives for a layout it refuses. A container's ordinary operations turn that into a panic,
and its `Try*` operations hand it to the caller.
Internal helpers; not part of the package API.

modules.name: CollectionError
modules.header:
Why a collection operation could not be completed.
Running out of memory is not one of the reasons: every container here terminates the program when its storage
cannot be had, and its `Try*` operations throw the allocator's own `AllocError` instead. What is left is the one
failure a caller can cause and act on, an index the collection does not have. An operation that cannot fail that
way reports an ordinary miss as an optional or a `bool`, so a rejected index is never mistaken for a missing key.
One rule holds everywhere: a failure means the receiver is unchanged. Nothing here leaves a collection
half-modified.

modules.name: Comparing
modules.header:
Ready-made ordering callbacks for the key types an ordered container is usually keyed on.
A tree takes its comparison as a function for the reason a table takes its hash as one: Rux has no closures, and
an interface value would be stored and dispatched through at every step of every descent — a dozen indirect calls
for a lookup that should be a dozen compares.
An ordering is one answer rather than two calls, which is why these return `Ordering` and not a pair of `<` and
`==` predicates. A descent asks one question per node and branches three ways on the answer.
A caller keying on a type not listed here writes its own. The rules are the ordinary ones: the comparison must be
consistent, must be the same every call, and must agree with equality — two keys that compare `Equal` are one key
as far as a tree is concerned, and the second one to arrive replaces the first.

modules.name: ContainerStorage
modules.header:
Talking to an allocator in elements rather than bytes.
Every container here holds a run of `T` and needs three things from an allocator: storage for a count of them,
storage of a different count with the old contents carried over, and the storage given back. Doing that by hand
means computing a layout at each site, and a layout computed wrongly is the defect that writes past the end of a
block the allocator thought was smaller. These helpers exist so it is computed once.
The layout comes from `sizeof(T)` and `alignof(T)`, asked of the element type at each instantiation. That is what
makes these usable by a container that has never seen an element and has none to hand: nothing here needs a sample
value.
A count of zero is not an error. It asks the allocator for a zero-sized block, which every allocator here answers
with a shared non-null aligned address, so an empty container is not a special shape and needs no null checks
downstream. That block must still be released, exactly like any other.
Internal to this package, and package-private so that it stays that way: these are the plumbing every container
shares, not something a caller reaches for. What a caller reaches for is a container, and what the plumbing does
is visible through one — a zero-sized element, a growth the allocator refuses, and the destruction of everything
held all show up at that surface, which is where Tests/Packages/Collections/ContainerStorage checks them.
Each request comes in two forms. `TryAllocateBlock` and `TryReallocateBlock` throw the `AllocError` for a container's
`Try*` operations to hand on; `AllocateBlock` and `ReallocateBlock` terminate the program instead, which is what
every other operation does when storage cannot be had.

modules.name: Deque
modules.header:
A double-ended queue over a circular buffer.
Elements go on and come off at either end in constant time, which is what a vector cannot offer at the front:
shifting every element along costs a linear pass per removal. This is the queue — `PushBack` and `PopFront` are
first in, first out — as `Vector` is the stack.
The capacity is always a power of two, or zero. That is what lets the ring wrap with a mask rather than a
division: logical element `i` lives at physical `(head + i) & (capacity - 1)`. Because the elements can straddle
the end of the block, a deque cannot always hand out one contiguous view; `AsSlices` gives the two runs without
moving anything, and `MakeContiguous` rotates them back together where one view is what a caller needs.
A deque owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. The allocator is
injected at construction and kept. Destruction destroys every element it holds and then releases the block.
Running out of memory terminates the program, as everywhere in this package. Growth allocates a fresh block,
relocates the elements into it, and only then releases the old one, so the elements are never anywhere but one
block. An operation given an index the deque does not have throws `IndexOutOfRange` and changes nothing.
The ring invariant, which every `Safety:` comment below leans on: `data` is null with `capacity` zero, or a block
from `AllocateBlock` with room for `capacity` elements, a power of two; `head < capacity`, `length <= capacity`, and
the `length` slots from `head` onward, wrapping, are initialized, so `SlotOf(i)` names one of them for `i < length`.

modules.name: HashMap
modules.header:
An associative table: keys to values, in no particular order, with constant expected time for everything.
Built on the `Table` kernel, so the probing, the displacement and the deletion are described there rather than
here. What this adds is the pair of callbacks that give a key type its identity, and the operations a caller
actually names.
The hash and equality are supplied rather than taken from the key type, because Rux has no closures and an
interface value would be stored and dispatched through on every lookup. `Hashing` has ready-made pairs for the
usual key types; a caller keying on its own type writes them, and the one rule is that keys comparing equal must
hash the same.
The hash is seeded, and the seed is drawn from `Rux/Entropy` unless the caller supplies one. That is what stops an
adversary who chooses keys from computing a few thousand that collide and turning every lookup into a scan.
A map owns its keys and values, so it prohibits copying and is move-only. Entries are destroyed when the map is,
when they are cleared, and when they are replaced — but not when they are removed, which hands the value back
instead.
Running out of memory terminates the program, as everywhere in this package; `TryInsert` and `TryReserve` throw
the allocator's `AllocError` instead and leave the map exactly as it was. So does a run of keys colliding so badly
that no table could place them, which only a broken hash produces; that is reported as `Unsupported`.

modules.name: HashSet
modules.header:
A set of distinct values, in no particular order, with constant expected time for everything.
The same `Table` kernel as `HashMap`, with nothing stored alongside each key. A set is a map whose values carry no
information, and saying so in the type rather than duplicating the probing is what keeps the two in step: a fix to
the displacement or the deletion is a fix to both.
The hash and equality are supplied for the same reason they are there, and the seed is drawn the same way.
A set owns its elements, so it prohibits copying and is move-only.
Running out of memory terminates the program, as everywhere in this package, and so does a run of elements
colliding so badly that no table could place them.

modules.name: Hashing
modules.header:
Ready-made hash and equality callbacks for the key types a table is usually keyed on.
A table takes its hash as a function rather than through an interface, because Rux has no closures and an
interface value would have to be stored and dispatched through per lookup. The signature carries the table's seed
alongside the key, which is what makes the hashing randomized: two tables in one program hash the same key
differently, and neither is predictable to anyone who has not seen the seed.
Every hash here is `SipHash`, which is the one in `Rux/Hash` designed for exactly this. An adversary who chooses
keys can find collisions in any of the others by hand, and a table full of colliding keys is a table whose every
lookup is a linear scan — a denial of service against anything keyed on input it did not write. `SipHash` makes
finding those collisions as hard as guessing the seed.
A caller keying on a type not listed here writes the pair itself: a hash that reads the whole key and mixes the
seed in, and an equality that agrees with it. The one rule is the usual one — two keys that compare equal must
hash the same.

modules.name: Iteration
modules.header:
Walking a run of contiguous elements, which every container in this package can hand out a view of.
The compiler drives a `for` loop by shape: anything with a `Next` returning an `Option` is an iterator, and the
item type is whatever that option carries. That leaves the choice of item to the iterator, and there are three
worth having.
`ValueIterator` yields elements by copy, which is what reading a sequence of numbers wants and what a move-only
element type must not be walked with — copying one would give two owners to a value that promises one.
`ReferenceIterator` yields a pointer to each element, which works for any element type at all and is how a
move-only one is read without being moved.
`MutableReferenceIterator` yields a writable pointer to each element, allowing in-place changes without copying.
All three borrow. None owns the storage it walks, and none may outlive the container it came from or survive that
container growing, rehashing or being freed — which is the one thing about iteration in this package worth
remembering.
A consuming iterator, which moves elements out of a container and leaves it empty, belongs to the container that
can be emptied rather than here.

modules.name: LruCache
modules.header:
A map of bounded size that forgets the entry used least recently when it has to make room.
Entries live in a vector and are linked into a list from the most to the least recently used; a hash map from each
key to its entry's index finds an entry in constant expected time. Looking an entry up or putting it moves it to the
front, and putting a new key into a full cache reuses the entry at the back, so a cache never allocates once it has
held as many entries as it may.

modules.name: Presentation
modules.header:
Showing what a sequential container holds, without disturbing it.
A container cannot implement `Debug` itself: what a `Vector<T>` looks like is entirely a question about `T`, and
an interface implementation has nowhere to say "when the element can be shown". So these are handwritten
functions carrying the bound — `WriteVectorDebug<T: Debug>` — which is the shape the language does have. Each
instantiation resolves its element's `WriteDebug` at compile time; nothing is dispatched at run time.
They borrow, and that is the whole design. A container owns its elements and hands out no copies of a move-only
one, so a diagnostic that took an element out to print it would be taking ownership of it — which is exactly what
a caller with a container they still need cannot afford. Every element here is shown through a borrow of it, so a
vector of a move-only type can be written as many times as wanted and still holds everything afterwards.
A vector and an array are one run of elements, so both hand `Rux/Text` their slice and it does the rest. A deque
is the exception, and the reason is its shape rather than an oversight: its elements live in a ring, so a deque
that has wrapped holds them in two runs with a gap between. It writes them as one sequence — which is what they
are to a reader — by walking both runs inside one pair of brackets, which is the one thing the slice writer
cannot be asked to do.
Maps and sets are here too, written `{key: value, key: value}` and `{element, element}` — braces rather than
brackets, because what a map holds is not a run of things and reading one as a sequence would be reading it
wrongly. The two kinds differ in exactly one respect, and it is the only interesting question they raise.
An ordered map or set is written in key order, which is the order it keeps and the order every walk of it takes,
so its rendering is a fact about its contents and nothing else. A hash map or set is written in the order of its
table, which is a fact about the container rather than about what it holds: it follows from the seed drawn when
the container was made and from every insertion and removal since, because displacement decides which of two
entries that want the same slot gets it. So two containers holding exactly the same entries render differently,
and so does the same container in the next run of the same program. That is documented rather than fixed: sorting
would need an ordering on the key that a hash container does not have and was built not to need, and inventing
one would make every hash container require something extra just so that its diagnostic looked tidy. A caller who
needs a stable order has an ordered map.
`CollectionError` presents itself here as well, for the same reason the containers do — this package depends on
`Rux/Text` and Text does not depend on it, so this is the side of the edge the implementation can live on.
`Display` is the description a reader is shown and `Debug` names the case, exactly as for the errors Text
presents. The descriptions are stable and are not a parsing contract: a program branches on the case.

modules.name: PriorityQueue
modules.header:
A queue that always hands out its largest element first.
The elements live in a vector arranged as a binary max-heap, so a push and a pop each cost time logarithmic in the
length and the largest element is always at the front. The sifting moves elements rather than copying them, so a
queue can hold elements that own something. "Largest" is the element type's `<`: a queue that should hand out the
smallest first holds elements whose `<` is reversed, which keeps the order part of the type rather than a function
every queue has to carry.

modules.name: SmallVector
modules.header:
A vector that keeps its first few elements inside itself, and only allocates past them.
The inline room is 64 bytes, as many elements as fit there at an alignment of at most eight; an element type that
is larger or more strictly aligned gets no inline room and behaves as a `Vector`. The room is raw words rather than
an array of elements, so nothing is ever destroyed that was never constructed. Once the elements outgrow it they
move to a block from the allocator and stay there.
Moving a small vector moves its inline elements with it, so a view or pointer into one lasts only until the vector
itself moves, as well as until it next changes.
The small-vector invariant, which every `Safety:` comment below leans on: while `heap` is null the first `length`
elements live in the inline room and `length <= InlineCapacity()`; once it is not, they live in `heap`, a block from
the allocator with room for `heapCapacity >= length` elements. Either way `Items()` and `WritableItems()` address
them.

modules.name: Table
modules.header:
The open-addressing kernel `HashMap` and `HashSet` are both built on, so the probe sequence, the displacement rule
and the deletion exist once rather than twice.
**Robin Hood.** Every entry records how far it sits from the slot its hash names — its probe distance. An
insertion that meets an entry closer to home than itself takes the slot and carries that entry onward, so the
distances along a chain never decrease and the worst one stays near the average. That is what keeps a lookup
bounded even when a table is nearly full, where plain linear probing degrades into a long scan of somebody else's
chain.
It also makes a miss cheap. A search that reaches a slot whose occupant is closer to home than the search has
travelled can stop there: the key it is looking for would have taken that slot on the way past. No tombstone, no
scan to the end of the chain.
**Backward-shift deletion.** Removing an entry moves the following ones back one slot each, stopping at an empty
slot or one already at home. That leaves the table exactly as if the removed entry had never been inserted --
there are no tombstones here at all, so a table that is churned rather than grown does not slowly fill with them
and rehash for no reason.
**Randomized hashing.** The hash a table uses is seeded, and the seed is a secret drawn from `Rux/Entropy`.
Without it, an adversary who chooses keys can compute a few thousand that collide and turn every lookup linear,
which is a denial of service against anything keying a table on input it did not write. The seeded hashers in
`Hashing` use `SipHash`, which is what makes guessing the seed the only way in.
Occupancy lives in the distance byte rather than in the key, so there is no reserved or sentinel key: every
possible `K` is storable, including zero and `uint::Max` and any struct bit pattern.
**Hash tags.** Each slot also keeps the top byte of its key's hash. A lookup compares that byte before it compares
keys, so a probe that passes other keys reads one byte for each instead of calling `equals` on it, which for text
keys means touching memory elsewhere. Only one key in 256 that differs gets as far as `equals`.
Internal to this package: the kernel, not something a caller reaches for.
The table invariant, which every `Safety:` comment below leans on: `capacity` is zero, with all four runs null, or
a power of two with each run allocated for `capacity` slots; every slot below `capacity` has its state byte written,
and its key, value and tag are initialized exactly when that byte is not `SlotEmpty`. Since the capacity is a power
of two, `HomeOf` and `NextOf` always name a slot below it.

modules.name: Tree
modules.header:
The red-black kernel `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` are both built on, so the rotations and the two fix-ups exist once
rather than twice.
A red-black tree keeps its entries in order and its height within twice the best possible, by colouring each node
and holding to four rules: the root is black, a red node has no red child, every path from a node down to a
missing child crosses the same number of black nodes, and a missing child counts as black. Insertion and removal
each break one of those locally, and each has a fix-up that walks back up until it is true again.
What that buys over a hash table is order. A tree walks its entries smallest first, answers what the least key
above a bound is, and never rehashes — so a walk stays meaningful across insertions in a way a table's cannot,
since a table moves entries between slots whenever it grows. What it costs is a pointer chase per level and an
allocation per entry, against the table's single run of memory and constant expected time. Reach for the tree when
order is part of the question, and the table when it is not.
Each node is its own allocation, which is what lets a node keep its address while the tree is rearranged around
it. Removal relinks the successor rather than copying its contents over the removed node, so the entry that stays
keeps the address it had. A table cannot promise that at all.
Every comparison goes through a function the caller supplies, for the reason the hash tables take theirs: Rux has
no closures, and an interface would be dispatched through at every step of every descent.
Internal to this package: the kernel, not something a caller reaches for.
The tree invariant, which every `Safety:` comment below leans on: `root` and every `left`, `right` and `parent`
link reachable from it is either null or a live node this tree allocated with `AllocateBlock` and has not yet given
back. Only `Attach` links nodes in and only `Detach` and `Clear` release them, so the invariant holds between calls.

modules.name: TreeMap
modules.header:
A map that keeps its keys in order.
`HashMap` is the one to reach for by default: it answers a lookup in constant expected time and this one takes a
pointer chase per level. What this offers instead is order. It walks its entries smallest key first, answers what
the nearest key above or below a bound is, and hands back everything between two bounds — none of which a hash
table can do at all, since a hash scatters keys on purpose and moves them between slots whenever it grows.
The ordering is the caller's, given once as a function and used for every descent. It has to be consistent, the
same every call, and agree with equality: two keys that compare `Equal` are one key here, and the second to
arrive replaces the first's value. `Comparing` has ready-made ones for the usual key types.
The balancing, the node ownership and the ordered walk are `Tree`'s; this is the map's shape over them.

modules.name: TreeSet
modules.header:
A set that keeps its elements in order.
`HashSet` answers membership in constant expected time and is the one to reach for by default. This one costs a
pointer chase per level and gives back order: it walks smallest first, answers what the nearest element above or
below a bound is, and hands back everything between two bounds. A hash set can do none of that, because a hash
scatters elements on purpose.
Order also changes what the algebra costs. Two hash sets can only be compared by looking every element of one up
in the other; two ordered sets could be merged in one pass. That merge is not what runs here — the predicates
below still ask `Contains` per element — because a merge needs both walks to survive the other's removals, and
what it would save is a logarithm. The operations that change a set do exploit the order, by asking for the next
element by key rather than by pointer, which is what lets them remove while walking.
The elements are the keys of a tree whose values are nothing at all. The unit `()` occupies no bytes, so a set is
a map with the values compiled away rather than a second copy of the same balancing.
An element must be copyable, for the same reason a `HashSet`'s must: the comparison takes its two elements by
value, and every descent compares against elements the set is holding. An element that owned something would be
handed to the comparison and destroyed there, taking what it owned with it. A set of owning values needs a
comparison that borrows, and there is no way to spell one that also works for the copyable case; until there is,
put the owning values in a `TreeMap` under keys that are copyable.

modules.name: Vector
modules.header:
A contiguous run of elements that grows as things are appended to it.
`Vector<T>` is the container to reach for by default. It is the stack — `Push` and `Pop` work at the end that
costs nothing to reach — and it is what a sequence of unknown length is built into before anything else looks at
it. `Array<T>` is what it becomes when the length stops changing.
A vector owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. Handing one to a function
requires an explicit move. Destruction destroys every element it
holds and then releases the block; the spare capacity past the length holds nothing and is not touched.
The allocator is injected at construction and kept, so a vector built from an arena disappears with the arena.
Capacity doubles rather than growing by a constant, which is what makes a run of appends cost an amortized
constant each rather than a reallocation every time. Capacity is never reduced except by `ShrinkToFit`, so a
vector that has been large stays cheap to refill.
`Push` moves its argument in rather than copying it, so a vector is how a sequence of elements that own something
is built: each is moved in exactly once and destroyed exactly once, when the vector is.
Running out of memory terminates the program, as everywhere in this package: `Push`, `Reserve` and every other
operation that may allocate either gets its storage or does not return. `TryPush`, `TryReserve` and `TryClone` are
for code that can recover; they throw the allocator's `AllocError` and leave the vector exactly as it was. An
operation that cannot allocate reports an ordinary miss as `none`, whether it hands back a value or a reference to
an element, and one given an index the vector does not have throws `IndexOutOfRange`.
The vector invariant, which every `Safety:` comment below leans on: `data` is null with `capacity` zero, or a block
from `AllocateBlock` or `ReallocateBlock` with room for `capacity` elements, and `length <= capacity` of them,
counting from the front, are initialized.

An empty vector with room for `capacity` elements already taken.
`allocator` is borrowed for the call and kept. The vector starts empty — capacity is not length. Terminates
the program when the storage cannot be had.

params.name: capacity
params.markdown: how many elements to make room for

doc.returns: an empty vector with room for that many elements already taken

members.signature: pub func FromSlice(allocator: Allocator, items: T[..]) -> Vector<T>

doc.summary: A vector holding a copy of every element of `items`, in order.
doc.markdown:
A vector holding a copy of every element of `items`, in order.
`allocator` is borrowed for the call and kept; `items` is borrowed and read. Copies its elements, so a move-only
element type is built with `Push` instead. Terminates the program when the storage cannot be had.
doc.returns: a vector holding a copy of those elements

doc.summary: An independent vector holding a copy of every element of this one.
doc.markdown:
An independent vector holding a copy of every element of this one.
`self` is borrowed and left alone. The copy takes exactly the room it needs rather than matching this one's
capacity, since the spare holds nothing worth reproducing.
Elements are copied with `=`, so the element type must be plain data that `Core::Copyable` describes; an
owning element type is rejected while compiling, at the copy. Terminates the program when the storage cannot
be had; `TryClone` reports that instead.
doc.returns: an independent copy

doc.markdown:
An independent vector holding a copy of every element of this one, or why the storage could not be had.
`self` is borrowed and left alone, whether or not the copy is made. Copies exactly as `Clone` does.
doc.returns: an independent copy, or throws the allocator's refusal

doc.markdown:
How many elements the vector holds.

doc.markdown:
How many elements the storage could hold without growing.
`self` is borrowed. Never below the length, and never reduced except by `ShrinkToFit`.
doc.returns: how many elements fit before the next growth

doc.summary: Whether the vector holds no elements.
doc.markdown:
Whether the vector holds no elements.
`self` is borrowed. A vector with capacity and no elements is empty: capacity is not length.
doc.returns: whether it holds nothing

members.signature: pub func Reserve(&var self, additional: uint)

doc.summary: Makes room for `additional` more elements on top of those already present.
doc.markdown:
Makes room for `additional` more elements on top of those already present.
`self` is borrowed mutably; the length does not change. Capacity only grows here; `ShrinkToFit` is what hands
it back. Terminates the program when the storage cannot be had, including when the current length plus
`additional` cannot be represented; `TryReserve` reports both instead.

params.name: additional
params.markdown: how many more elements to make room for

members.name: TryReserve
members.signature: pub func TryReserve(&var self, additional: uint) throws AllocError

doc.summary: Makes room for `additional` more elements on top of those already present, or throws why it could not.
doc.markdown:
Makes room for `additional` more elements on top of those already present, or throws why it could not.
`self` is borrowed mutably; the length does not change. A failure leaves the vector exactly as it was.
Throws `Unsupported` when the current length plus `additional` cannot be represented, which is what turns a
`TryReserve(uint::Max)` on a non-empty vector into a reported error rather than a silently tiny capacity, and
otherwise whatever the allocator refused with.

params.name: additional
params.markdown: how many more elements to make room for

doc.returns: nothing, or throws the allocator's refusal

doc.summary: Releases the capacity past the length.
doc.markdown:
Releases the capacity past the length.
`self` is borrowed mutably. A vector with nothing in it gives up its storage entirely and becomes as cheap as
a new one. Terminates the program when the allocator refuses to move the elements into the smaller block.

doc.summary: Destroys every element, keeping the storage.
doc.markdown:
Destroys every element, keeping the storage.
`self` is borrowed mutably. The vector is empty afterwards and can be refilled without allocating again.
Runs in time proportional to the length.

members.name: Truncate
members.signature: pub func Truncate(&var self, length: uint)

doc.summary: Destroys the elements past `length`, keeping the storage.
doc.markdown:
Destroys the elements past `length`, keeping the storage.
`self` is borrowed mutably. A `length` at or past the current one changes nothing, so this never grows.
This is the other half of the `Rux/Algorithms` seam: `Unique`, `RemoveWhere`, `RemoveValue` and `Partition`
compact survivors toward the front and report the surviving length without resizing anything, and this is how
a vector is told about it.
Runs in time proportional to how many elements go.

doc.summary: Destroys every element and releases the storage.
doc.markdown:
Destroys every element and releases the storage.
Runs when the vector's life ends. The spare capacity past the length holds nothing and is not touched; the
elements go first and the block second, since an element destroyed after its storage was released would be
read from freed memory.

members.signature: pub func Push(&var self, value: T)

doc.summary: Appends one element, growing the storage when it is full.
doc.markdown:
Appends one element, growing the storage when it is full.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `value` is read by value and moved into the vector. Terminates the program when
the storage cannot grow; `TryPush` reports that instead.
Amortized constant time: the doubling is what spreads the cost of growing across the appends that caused it.

members.name: TryPush
members.signature: pub func TryPush(&var self, value: T) throws AllocError

doc.summary: Appends one element, growing the storage when it is full, or throws why the storage could not grow.
doc.markdown:
Appends one element, growing the storage when it is full, or throws why the storage could not grow.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `value` is read by value and moved into the vector. A failure leaves the vector
exactly as it was, and `value` is then destroyed here.
Amortized constant time, as `Push` is.
doc.returns: nothing, or throws the allocator's refusal

members.signature: pub func PushSlice(&var self, items: T[..])

doc.summary: Appends a copy of every element of `items`, in order.
doc.markdown:
Appends a copy of every element of `items`, in order.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `items` is borrowed and read. Room for all of them is taken first, so this either
appends every element or terminates the program before appending any.

doc.summary: Takes the last element out of the vector.
doc.markdown:
Takes the last element out of the vector.
`self` is borrowed mutably; the element is moved out rather than copied, so this is how an element that owns
something leaves a vector without being destroyed. Reports `none` and changes nothing when the vector is empty.
The storage is kept, so a vector emptied this way costs nothing to refill.
doc.returns: the removed element, or `none` when the vector is empty

doc.markdown:
The element at `index`, or `none` when there is no such index.
`self` is borrowed; the element is returned by copy.
doc.returns: a copy of the element, or `none` when the index is out of range

doc.summary: The element at `index`, borrowed where it sits, or `none` when there is no such index.
doc.markdown:
The element at `index`, borrowed where it sits, or `none` when there is no such index.
`self` stays borrowed while the reference is in use, so the vector cannot grow, shrink, or be destroyed under
it.
doc.returns: a reference to the element, or `none` when the index is out of range

members.signature: pub func AtMutable(&var self, index: uint) -> &var T?

doc.markdown:
The element at `index`, borrowed to be written where it sits, or `none` when there is no such index.
`self` stays borrowed exclusively while the reference is in use.
doc.returns: a writable reference to the element, or `none` when the index is out of range

members.name: Set
members.signature: pub func Set(&var self, index: uint, value: T) throws CollectionError

doc.summary: Replaces the element at `index` with `value`, destroying the element that was there.
doc.markdown:
Replaces the element at `index` with `value`, destroying the element that was there.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `value` is moved in. The old element is destroyed once the new one is in place,
so an element that owns something is released rather than leaked; `Replace` hands it back instead. Reports
`IndexOutOfRange` and changes nothing when there is no such index, and `value` is then destroyed here.
doc.returns: nothing when the element was written, or `IndexOutOfRange`

members.signature: pub func Replace(&var self, index: uint, value: T) -> T throws CollectionError

doc.markdown:
Replaces the element at `index` with `value` and hands back the element that was there.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `value` is moved in and the old element is moved out to the caller rather than
destroyed. Reports `IndexOutOfRange` and changes nothing when there is no such index, and `value` is then
destroyed here.
doc.returns: the element that was at `index`, or `IndexOutOfRange`

doc.summary: The initialized elements as a borrowed read-only view.
doc.markdown:
The initialized elements as a borrowed read-only view.
`self` is borrowed. Never the spare capacity, which holds nothing.
The view is valid until the vector grows, shrinks, or is destroyed.
doc.returns: the elements, borrowed

members.signature: pub func AsMutableSlice(&var self) -> var T[..]

doc.summary: The initialized elements as a borrowed writable view.
doc.markdown:
The initialized elements as a borrowed writable view.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Never the spare capacity.
The view is valid until the vector grows, shrinks, or is destroyed.
doc.returns: the elements, borrowed for writing

doc.summary: An iterator over the elements, by copy.
doc.markdown:
An iterator over the elements, by copy.
`self` is borrowed and must outlive the iterator. This is the method a `for` loop finds.
The vector must not grow or shrink while the iterator is alive.
doc.returns: a cursor yielding copies of the elements

doc.summary: An iterator over pointers to the elements.
doc.markdown:
An iterator over pointers to the elements.
`self` is borrowed and must outlive the iterator.
doc.returns: a cursor yielding the elements' addresses

doc.summary: An iterator over writable pointers to initialized elements, without copying them.
doc.markdown:
An iterator over writable pointers to initialized elements, without copying them.
The vector's storage must outlive the iterator and every yielded pointer. Do not grow, shrink, destroy, or
move the vector while any of them is in use, and coordinate aliases that access the same elements.
doc.returns: a cursor yielding writable element addresses

members.name: Insert
members.signature: pub func Insert(&var self, index: uint, value: T) throws CollectionError

doc.summary: Inserts `value` at `index`, moving everything from there on one place along.
doc.markdown:
Inserts `value` at `index`, moving everything from there on one place along.
`self` is borrowed mutably; `value` is moved in. An `index` equal to the length appends, which is what makes
the rejection above it a boundary rather than a blanket refusal; anything past that reports
`IndexOutOfRange` and changes nothing.
Terminates the program when the storage cannot grow.
Runs in time proportional to how many elements follow the insertion point.
doc.returns: nothing when the element was inserted, or `IndexOutOfRange`

members.name: RemoveAt
members.signature: pub func RemoveAt(&var self, index: uint) -> T?

doc.summary: Takes the element at `index` out, moving everything after it one place back.
doc.markdown:
Takes the element at `index` out, moving everything after it one place back.
`self` is borrowed mutably. The element is moved out and handed to the caller rather than destroyed, so an
element that owns something leaves intact. Reports `none` and changes nothing when there is no such index.
Order is preserved, which is what separates this from `SwapRemoveAt`. Runs in time proportional to how many
elements follow the one removed.
doc.returns: the element removed, or `none` when the index is out of range

members.name: SwapRemoveAt
members.signature: pub func SwapRemoveAt(&var self, index: uint) -> T?

doc.summary: Takes the element at `index` out and moves the last one into its place.
doc.markdown:
Takes the element at `index` out and moves the last one into its place.
`self` is borrowed mutably. The element is moved out and handed to the caller. Reports `none` and changes
nothing when there is no such index.
Order is *not* preserved — whatever was last now sits where the removed element was — and that is the whole
point: this is constant time where `RemoveAt` is linear, and for a sequence nobody is reading in order the
difference is free.
doc.returns: the element removed, or `none` when the index is out of range

doc.summary: The first element, borrowed where it sits, or `none` for an empty vector.
doc.markdown:
The first element, borrowed where it sits, or `none` for an empty vector.
`self` stays borrowed while the reference is in use.
doc.returns: a reference to the first element, or `none` when empty

doc.summary: The last element, borrowed where it sits, or `none` for an empty vector.
doc.markdown:
The last element, borrowed where it sits, or `none` for an empty vector.
`self` stays borrowed while the reference is in use.
doc.returns: a reference to the last element, or `none` when empty

members.name: Slice
members.signature: pub func Slice(&self, start: uint, count: uint) -> T[..]

doc.summary: A borrowed read-only view of `count` elements starting at `start`.
doc.markdown:
A borrowed read-only view of `count` elements starting at `start`.
`self` is borrowed. A `start` at or past the length gives an empty view, and a `count` running past the end is
clamped, so the result never covers storage the vector does not hold.
The view is valid until the vector grows, shrinks, or is destroyed.
doc.returns: that run of elements, borrowed; empty when the range is out of bounds

members.name: MutableSliceOf
members.signature: pub func MutableSliceOf(&var self, start: uint, count: uint) -> var T[..]

doc.summary: A borrowed writable view of `count` elements starting at `start`.
doc.markdown:
A borrowed writable view of `count` elements starting at `start`.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Clamped exactly as `Slice` is.
The view is valid until the vector grows, shrinks, or is destroyed.
doc.returns: that run borrowed for writing; empty when the range is out of bounds

doc.summary: Takes the vector apart into an iterator over its elements.
doc.markdown:
Takes the vector apart into an iterator over its elements.
Consumes the vector: it is moved into the iterator, and the storage goes with it, so nothing is copied and
nothing is reallocated. Each element comes out by value, which is how one that owns something leaves.
Whatever is not taken is destroyed when the iterator's life ends.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: a cursor that consumes the vector as it goes

doc.summary: Copies the elements into a fixed-length array.
doc.markdown:
Copies the elements into a fixed-length array.
`self` is borrowed and keeps its own storage, so both are released independently. Copies its elements, so this
is for element types where copying means what it says — `IntoArray` is what moves them. Terminates the
program when the storage cannot be had.
doc.returns: an array holding a copy of the elements

doc.summary: Hands the storage itself to a fixed-length array, copying nothing.
doc.markdown:
Hands the storage itself to a fixed-length array, copying nothing.
Consumes the vector. The spare capacity is trimmed first, and the trim has to succeed: an array releases its
block with the layout of its length, so a block still carrying spare capacity would be given back under a layout
it was not taken with. A trim the allocator refuses terminates the program, as `ShrinkToFit` does; it is close
to impossible, since it asks for less than the block already holds.
doc.returns: an array taking the vector's storage rather than copying it

doc.summary: An iterator that takes a vector apart, yielding each element by value.
doc.markdown:
An iterator that takes a vector apart, yielding each element by value.
Move-only: it owns the storage the vector owned, prohibits copying, and destroys it with `~VectorIntoIterator`.
This is how a vector of elements that
own something is emptied into somewhere else — each element is moved out rather than copied, and whatever is
left when the iterator's life ends is destroyed with it.

fields.doc: The storage taken from the vector.

fields.doc: How many have been yielded.

doc.summary: Destroys whatever was not yielded and releases the storage.
doc.markdown:
Destroys whatever was not yielded and releases the storage.
Runs when the iterator's life ends. Everything already yielded belongs to whoever took it and is not touched
here, which is what makes stopping part-way through safe.

doc.summary: The next element, moved out, or `none` once every element has been yielded.
doc.markdown:
The next element, moved out, or `none` once every element has been yielded.
`self` is borrowed mutably and advanced. The element is moved rather than copied, so it is the caller's to
keep or destroy; an exhausted iterator keeps reporting `none`.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the next element, or `none` at the end
